stories.title: Platform-independent SIMD in Go
stories.snippet: Go 1.27 adds an experimental platform-agnostic SIMD API
stories.summary: Go 1.26 and 1.27 include experimental SIMD APIs, with Go 1.27 introducing a portable, platform-agnostic simd package loosely based on Highway for C++. This package hides architectural differences by removing fixed-size vectors from the type system and supporting only operations common to all platforms, filling gaps with efficient emulation. It supports AVX, AVX2, and AVX512 on amd64, NEON on arm64, and wasm SIMD instructions, while emulating operations on platforms lacking SIMD support. Vector types are capitalized plurals like simd.Uint8s or simd.Float32s, loaded from and stored to slices, and the package includes arithmetic, comparison, conversion, shift, and masking operations. The experimental package is enabled with GOEXPERIMENT=simd, and ReduceSum is planned for a future release to allow cross-element vector reduction.

stories.title: AI-powered fuzzing with the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent
stories.snippet: In this blog post, I explain how to use the new fuzzing taskflow based on the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent AI framework. The post AI-powered fuzzing with the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: GitHub Security Lab's Fuzzing Taskflow is an autonomous fuzzing pipeline for C/C++ projects built on the Taskflow Agent framework. Pointed at a GitHub repository, the agent identifies entrypoints, analyzes the build system, writes harnesses, runs AFL++, interprets coverage reports, improves harnesses, triages crashes, and generates vulnerability reports without human intervention. The architecture separates decision-making from execution, with the LLM agent choosing what to fuzz while MCP tools handle compilation and AFL runs, and all state is persisted in a SQLite database. Each harness is compiled twice—once with AFL's edge instrumentation for fuzzing and once with clang's coverage mapping for human-readable reports—and the feedback loop uses plateau detection to stop when two consecutive iterations gain less than 1% line coverage. Time budgets double each round from 30 seconds to roughly 32 minutes per target, and the pipeline also ships structure-aware mutators and a persistent, deduplicated corpus that survives across iterations.

stories.title: When chat is the wrong UI
stories.snippet: What is a developer to do when they need something more tangible than a chat box? Enter canvases. The post When chat is the wrong UI appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: The article by Burke Holland argues that chat interfaces are often the wrong way to interact with AI, since they push users to rely on the agent itself as the tool rather than having it build dedicated tools. He proposes "canvases" as an alternative: full-stack applications that run inside the GitHub Copilot app and communicate bi-directionally with the Copilot agent. Canvases can call third-party APIs, execute code locally on the user's machine, and serve as customizable interfaces for specific tasks. Examples include a Connect 4 game, a Winget package manager UI, a SQLite database tool, and a blog post editor. Holland suggests using canvases to automate development workflows through stages of research, prototyping, planning, implementation, iteration, and finalization, allowing users to step away from the loop as much as possible.

stories.title: Rendering huge pull requests in the GitHub Copilot app
stories.snippet: How we rebuilt the diff surface in the GitHub Copilot app to open a million-line pull request with hundreds of inline review comments. The post Rendering huge pull requests in the GitHub Copilot app appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: The GitHub Copilot app rebuilt its pull request view to handle extremely large PRs, testing it on an open-source pull request with 2,200 files, over a million changed lines, and more than 400 inline review comments. Code rows are easy to virtualize because their heights are deterministic and known upfront, but comments are not, since their height depends on markdown wrapping, expandable sections, reply composers, and async-loading images that only reveal themselves at render time. To solve this, the team split the document's geometry into two independent domains: a deterministic code height computed exactly, and dynamic block heights that are estimated, then measured lazily, anchored to file, line, and side rather than pixel coordinates. They rejected a per-block ResizeObserver design because it created feedback loops, and instead shipped a single idle- and scroll-gated measurement pass scoped to the viewport. On-screen blocks are treated as ground truth and read in batch, with one exception where user-caused resizes like expanding a details block apply corrections in the same frame.

stories.title: An Analytical Theory of Auxiliary Learning
stories.snippet: Auxiliary learning is an optimization paradigm in which a neural network's performance on a target task is improved by jointly training it on additional tasks. stories.summary: The paper develops an analytical theory to explain auxiliary learning, an optimization paradigm in which training on additional tasks improves a neural network's performance on a target task. Using a teacher-student framework, the authors derive a closed system of differential equations describing the dynamics of online stochastic gradient descent in the large-input limit. For linear networks, they obtain a closed-form expression for generalization error to leading order in the learning rate, demonstrating how task correlations and label noise determine the benefit of auxiliary learning. For non-linear activation functions, they introduce a fluctuation-dissipation analytical theory linking main and auxiliary errors to the corresponding single-task error. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions, showing that auxiliary tasks improve generalization by balancing the forcing dynamics toward the optimal solution against gradient noise.

stories.title: CORDIAL: Calibrating Ordinal LLM Outputs from Few Labels
stories.snippet: A large language model (LLM) can turn a text into a distribution over an ordered scale, but that distribution is a noisy measurement: saturated, compressed or exaggerated, and biased in a consistent direction. We propose CORDIAL, which treats the model's output as a noisy reading of the true label and corrects it with a channel of five interpretable parameters. The channel is small enough for its posterior to be averaged from a handful of labels, and we prove that the resulting calibration preserves first-order stochastic order. On Amazon reviews and CMU-MOSEI transcripts with four LLMs, CORDIAL has the lowest log loss among nine calibrators in 76 of 80 settings with 5 to 100 labels; with 20 labels and the main 7B reader, it matches the strongest baseline using 28-54 labels. stories.summary: CORDIAL is a calibration method proposed by Wang, Wang, and Halgamuge that corrects noisy ordinal outputs from large language models using a small channel of five interpretable parameters. The approach treats the model's output distribution as a noisy reading of the true label and is small enough that its posterior can be averaged from just a handful of labels, while provably preserving first-order stochastic order. Evaluated on Amazon reviews and CMU-MOSEI transcripts across four LLMs, CORDIAL achieved the lowest log loss among nine calibrators in 76 of 80 settings when using between 5 and 100 labels. With only 20 labels and the main 7B reader, it matched the strongest baseline's performance that required 28 to 54 labels. The same posterior framework also enables transferring priors learned from other tasks and fusing outputs from multiple LLMs, with unrestricted calibrators such as Dirichlet calibration only surpassing it once the calibration set grows into the hundreds or thousands.

stories.title: TopU-LBVS: A Realistic Multi Target Benchmark for Ligand Based Virtual Screening
stories.snippet: Ligand-based virtual screening (LBVS) is a practical first-pass tool in early-stage drug discovery, but existing benchmarks can overestimate performance through random negatives, easy decoys, limited target coverage, and non-standardized evaluation protocols. We introduce TopU-LBVS, a multi-target benchmark for LBVS under hard-negative screening conditions. Starting from curated ChEMBL~35 bioactivity data, TopU-LBVS covers 93 protein targets across 7 protein classes and constructs target-specific screening libraries with property-matched, structurally similar decoys at a fixed 1:40 active-to-decoy ratio. stories.summary: TopU-LBVS is a multi-target benchmark designed to evaluate ligand-based virtual screening (LBVS) under realistic hard-negative conditions, addressing limitations in existing benchmarks such as random negatives, easy decoys, limited target coverage, and non-standardized protocols. Built from curated ChEMBL~35 bioactivity data, the benchmark spans 93 protein targets across 7 protein classes, with target-specific screening libraries containing property-matched, structurally similar decoys at a fixed 1:40 active-to-decoy ratio and compound counts ranging from roughly 400 to 10,000. The benchmark provides three fixed protocols: TopU-LBVS-full for cross-target generalization, TopU-LBVS-low for low-data learning within the hard-negative distribution, and TopU-LBVS-mini, a compact seven-target protocol paired with a random-decoy control. Across ten reference baselines spanning fingerprint methods, molecular GNNs, and modern molecular models, performance under random-decoy evaluation degrades sharply when tested with hard negatives. The authors release data, splits, evaluation code, and baseline implementations to enable reproducible comparison.

stories.title: WeatherDiagFlow: Evidence-Grounded Radar Nowcasting with Diagnostic Flow Refinement
stories.snippet: Radar nowcasting is essential for short-term warning and emergency response, yet conventional systems mainly return future radar fields and provide limited support for operational communication and post-event verification. We formulate radar nowcasting as an evidence-grounded forecast--bulletin--audit task, in which a numerical forecaster produces both future radar fields and structured diagnostic evidence. Forecast-time bulletins use only model-available evidence, whereas post-event audits incorporate future radar truth only after the forecast horizon is observed. stories.title: On Growth and Form, and Function: Reusable Regulatory Handles Control Phenotypic Variation

stories.summary: Inspired by D'Arcy Thompson's 1917 "On Growth and Form," researchers investigate how coherent large-scale transformations of morphology can be encoded as low-dimensional modulations of a self-organizing developmental system. They use neural cellular automata (NCAs) as bio-inspired models where a shared local regulatory network grows target morphologies from a single cell. Applying low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to pretrained NCAs, each developmental program is represented as a low-rank modulation of a fixed regulatory scaffold. Horizontal and vertical scaling of a fully grown 2D emoji phenotype can each be implemented by rank-one adaptations, whose linear combinations parametrically control phenotype size, generalize beyond the training distribution, and compose with target-specific adapters. Adaptations learned for one phenotype transfer zero-shot across structurally and semantically diverse phenotypes sharing the same scaffold while largely preserving internal features. From approximately 25,000 independently trained phenotype-specific NCA adapters, the authors identify latent low-dimensional directions that functionally control phenotypic variation including scaling, style, and symmetrical fission.

stories.title: WaveDigger: Dig into wireless signals to discover their physical locations
stories.summary: WaveDigger is a web application that locates the physical positions of Wi-Fi access points and cell towers using their network identifiers. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, and deck.gl, it allows users to search by BSSID (MAC address) for Wi-Fi access points or by parameters like MCC, MNC, TAC, and Cell ID/NCI for LTE and 5G NR towers, with 5G searches returning the target cell plus surrounding cells in the same cluster. The app features automatic BSSID input validation, interactive map visualization, search history tracking, and responsive design for desktop and mobile. It queries Apple's undocumented WLOC API using protobuf definitions and reverse-engineered protocols developed by the apple-corelocation-experiments team. A hosted version is available at wavedigger.networksurvey.app, and the project is licensed under AGPL v3.0, with a roadmap that includes export functionality and a TAC-cluster browsing view.

stories.title: Search – A small, fast WebKit browser for macOS
stories.summary: Search is a small macOS web browser built by Office Commun that uses Apple's WebKit engine, keeping its size to about 3 MB and enabling instant launches without bundling a second browser engine. It strips away toolbars, start pages, sidebars, and accounts, offering only a single field for addresses or searches plus a row of tabs that can sit across the top or down the left. Built-in features include a network-level ad blocker, per-site element hiding, reading mode, picture-in-picture video, and password storage in the macOS keychain, with Chrome extension support layered over WebKit's extension engine. All user data stays on the Mac with no sync, account, telemetry, or analytics, and the only outbound request is a daily update check. The browser's roughly 12,700 lines of Swift source are publicly available under an MIT license and can be built locally with swift build or ./build.sh.

stories.title: Show HN: Treepeat – Code similarity detection using Tree-sitter
stories.snippet: treepeat is a tool that finds similarities in your codebase. Find duplicate code blocks meaningful to the language (classes/functions), not just lines. Find near-duplicates: ignore whitespace, strings, high level AST nodes such as function and names. Find structurally similar code: anonymize identifiers, constants, etc. Pull requests welcome: This is very much an proof of concept - I'm happy with it, but I haven't supported very many languages at present. Languages supported: astro, bash, css, go, html, javascript, lua, markdown (plus codeblocks), python, sql, typescript, java, kotlin, rust, yaml
stories.summary: Treepeat is an open-source code similarity detection tool that uses Tree-sitter AST analysis and locality-sensitive hashing to identify duplicate and near-duplicate code blocks within a codebase. It offers three rulesets—none, default, and loose—that control normalization by either ignoring only whitespace and strings or fully anonymizing identifiers and constants. The tool supports numerous languages including Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Lua, SQL, Bash, CSS, HTML, and Astro, and is installed via pip. Its main detect command provides configurable flags such as --similarity for thresholds, --min-lines for match size, --diff for side-by-side comparisons, and --format sarif for CI integration. Additional subcommands include list-ruleset, which displays normalization rules, and treesitter, which shows how source code is normalized into tokens for debugging similarity results.

stories.title: Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats
stories.summary: In spring 2026, Anthropic formed a life sciences research group and tasked Claude with searching DNA databases for novel reverse transcriptase (RT) systems. Using roughly 950 agents and 210 million tokens over 21 hours, Claude gathered over 200,000 RTs, narrowed them to 3,500 candidates, and produced reports on the 20 most compelling. One agent detected a tandem repeat array next to an odd-looking RT, leading to the discovery of array-associated reverse transcriptases (ART), a previously uncharacterized system found mainly in bacteriophages. ART consists of an RT, a partner gene, and a CRISPR-like array of evenly spaced DNA repeats, with initial experiments showing the array is expressed as distinct short RNAs. Although the underlying RT had been identified in prior studies, Claude was the first to recognize the system's defining features, a finding Feng Zhang of MIT and the Broad Institute called an exciting example of AI contributing to biological discovery.
